summary: Alejandro Reuss's Dollars & Sense Econo FAQ explains why the Federal Reserve is buying long-term government bonds to push down long-term interest rates and stimulate investment and spending. It walks through how bond prices and yields move inversely, how lower risk-free rates are meant to pass through to risky loans via risk premiums, and why deflation and a weaker dollar are considered. The article concludes that the policy faces major obstacles, such as banks holding excess reserves and weak investment demand, and argues that fiscal stimulus such as higher unemployment insurance, state grants, infrastructure spending and direct hiring would be more effective.
one_line: Explains the Federal Reserve's purchase of long-term government bonds to lower long-term interest rates, and its doubtful effectiveness during the recession.
key_facts: The Federal Reserve buys long-term government bonds in order to push down long-term interest rates, which is meant to stimulate investment and other forms of spending.
The main way the Fed influences interest rates is by buying and selling government bonds; selling bonds raises interest rates and buying bonds lowers them.
Using a $100 bond that promises $110 in a year, the article computes a 10% interest rate, and shows that a $105 price implies an interest rate of less than 5%.
The U.S. government is treated as a risk-free borrower, and the difference between a risky loan's rate and the risk-free rate is called the 'risk premium.'
The federal funds rate, the interest rate banks charge each other on overnight loans, had basically been 0% for a couple of years when the article was written.
The article states that there are about 15 million unemployed workers, plus millions more working part-time who want full-time jobs.
Deflation would redistribute income from low-income debtors to high-income creditors, and would likely reduce overall spending because high-income people save more.
A weaker dollar makes U.S. exports cheaper for foreign buyers, and the article notes the governments of Germany and China criticized the Fed's plan.
The article notes that banks have held much of the new money as 'excess reserves' over and above legal requirements rather than lending it out.
The article argues that businesses have negative expectations of future sales and vast excess capacity, so lower interest rates are not very likely to entice new investment.
The article says the first fiscal stimulus 'was way too small' as serious economists pointed out at the time.

Proposed fiscal policies include increasing unemployment insurance payments, federal grants to prevent state budget cuts, additional government spending on infrastructure and alternative energy, and direct government hiring like the Works Progress Administration (WPA).
The article concludes that the reasons such fiscal policies seem unlikely lie in the distribution of political power rather than any inherent mystery.
Alejandro Reuss is described as an historian and economist and a member of the Dollars & Sense collective.

entities.name: Federal Reserve
entities.role: The central monetary-policy making authority for the United States, referred to as 'the Fed', which buys and sells government bonds to influence interest rates.

entities.name: U.S. Treasury
entities.role: Sells government bonds when the government needs to borrow; the bonds are later bought by the Fed.

entities.name: Alejandro Reuss
entities.role: Author of the article; described as an historian and economist and a member of the Dollars & Sense collective.

entities.name: Dollars & Sense
entities.role: Publication (Real World Economics) in which the web-only article appeared as part of the Econo FAQs series.

entities.name: Works Progress Administration (WPA)
entities.role: Example of direct government hiring during the Great Depression, cited as a model for current policy.

entities.name: federal funds rate
entities.role: Very short-term interest rate banks charge each other on overnight loans, which the Fed usually targets; basically 0% for a couple of years.

entities.name: Germany
entities.role: Country whose government criticized the Fed's plan, evidently fearing effects on its trade balance and exporting employment.

entities.role: Country whose government criticized the Fed's plan, evidently fearing effects on its trade balance and exporting employment.
